newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan says recovery slow, but sounds upbeat note.
newsitem.headline: Japan says recovery slow, but sounds upbeat note.

text.p: The government said on Tuesday that Japan's economic recovery remained slow, but it sounded a note of increased optimism by highlighting better output, especially of vehicles and communications-related products.
The overall phraseology of the Economic Planning Agency's (EPA) monthly economic report, which is closely watched by markets for signs of policy shift, was unchanged from November.
"Our country's economy continues to recover, although the pace of the recovery is slow," the December report said.
The EPA has for most of this year described Japan's economy as gradually recovering, despite some weakness after years of negligible growth.

But as a sign of the government's increasing optimism, the report noted that industrial production was increasing, moving a step forward from the previous month, when the EPA said output was "gradually" increasing.

The high pace of automobile production was the main element supporting output growth, an EPA official told reporters, adding a steady rise in output of communications-related products had also contributed to the overall growth.
The official said a fall in semiconductor production was bottoming out, but the outlook for a recovery of that sector was still uncertain.
The EPA's economic report said exports remained strong, due to increased exports of electrical equipment to Asian nations and of car parts.
"Recent economic data shows that Japan's economy is firming," EPA Minister Taro Aso told a news conference.

The EPA announced separately on Tuesday that Japan's private-sector machinery orders in October, excluding those for machinery at electrical power firms and for ships, rose 44.2 percent from September after a 10.2 percent fall that month.
Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita reiterated the central bank's view of the economy during a budget committee meeting in parliament.
"Japan's economy is continuing its gradual recovery and the strength of the recovery is becoming more firm," he said.

Asked what it would take for the government to move its assessment of the economy up a notch, the EPA official said: "The key is whether private demand will continue to show a steady rise at a time when public demand is shrinking."

He said capital investment had picked up, particularly in the latter half of the current fiscal year, and construction of new houses had risen at an unusually high pace due to demand before a planned sales tax increase next April.
Industrial production was also showing signs of a steady increase, and "the key is whether these (signs of increasing private demand) will continue in the future," he said.
November's report had retained the familiar reference to gradual economic recovery, but moved an inch forward by deleting the phrase "there are some worrying aspects" from its overall assessment.

December's report said bank lending had dropped from the previous year and government bond yields remained low. This reflected uncertainty in financial markets about the future of Japan's economy, despite signs of brightness in the real economy, the EPA official said.

"There is a consensus that the economic recovery is increasing its steadiness, but I believe the low yields in government bonds reflect the fact that neither the financial markets nor the economists have a clear picture of the future (of Japan's economy)," he said.
